ranking.rationale: Age is one of the strongest and most stable predictors of hypertension across populations and time, with clear causal relevance and low risk of acting as a domain identifier compared with state, year, race, or other potentially brittle shortcut features.

Diabetes is a strong, mechanistically related comorbidity/risk factor for hypertension and should remain predictive across BRFSS domains better than state, year, race, sex, or other likely shortcut variables. It adds substantial stable signal beyond age, whereas many lifestyle and access variables are weaker, noisier self-reports or more domain-sensitive.

Physical inactivity is a well-established, semantically stable risk factor for hypertension and adds complementary lifestyle information beyond age and diabetes. It is more likely to generalize across BRFSS domains than state/year identifiers or demographic shortcut variables, and is less brittle than access-to-care or survey-artifact features.

Cost-related barriers to care are a stable socioeconomic determinant linked to hypertension diagnosis and management, adding complementary signal beyond age, diabetes, and physical activity. It is more semantically tied to blood-pressure risk/control than diet or smoking here, while avoiding obvious domain-ID leakage from year/state and reducing reliance on demographic shortcut features like race or sex.

Sex is a well-established, biologically grounded predictor of hypertension risk that should remain predictive across BRFSS domains and adds complementary signal beyond age, diabetes, physical activity, and cost barriers. It is more stable and less domain-identifying than state or year, and less likely to act as a brittle socioeconomic or demographic shortcut than race, employment, or poverty.

Poverty adds stable socioeconomic risk information for hypertension beyond age, diabetes, activity, medical cost, and sex. It is more semantically tied to chronic stress, diet quality, and care access than year/state identifiers or race, and is less brittle than many lifestyle proxies or downstream health-status variables.

Smoking history is a well-established, semantically stable cardiovascular risk factor that adds health-behavior signal beyond age, diabetes, activity, sex, poverty, and cost barriers. It is less likely than state, year, race, or employment to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and is cleaner and more robust than current-smoking detail or alcohol variables.

Current smoking intensity/status adds stable cardiovascular risk information beyond ever-smoked history, improving on SMOKE100 with a more proximal exposure signal while remaining more semantically tied to blood-pressure risk than domain-heavy variables like STATE/IYEAR or shortcut-prone demographics.

Employment status adds stable health and functional-status signal beyond age, poverty, sex, smoking, activity, diabetes, and cost barriers. It is plausibly linked to hypertension through stress, disability, retirement, and ability to work, while being less domain-specific and less likely to encode benchmark split identifiers than survey year or state, and less shortcut-prone than race.

Alcohol consumption is a plausible, semantically stable behavioral risk factor for hypertension that adds health-related signal beyond age, diabetes, activity, smoking, sex, poverty, and employment. It is less likely than STATE or IYEAR to encode domain identity, and less likely than race or cancer-history variables to act as demographic shortcuts or weak, indirect proxies.

Vegetable consumption adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle signal for blood-pressure risk that complements age, diabetes, activity, smoking, alcohol, and socioeconomic variables already selected. It is more likely to generalize across domains than survey year/state, and is less prone to demographic shortcutting than race; it also offers broader cardiovascular relevance than the cancer-history variables.

Fruit intake adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle signal for blood-pressure risk that complements vegetables, activity, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, age, and poverty. It is more likely to generalize across domains than state/year and is less prone to demographic shortcutting than race; cancer history is less directly predictive, and binge drinking is partly redundant with drinks per week.

Binge drinking adds a plausible, behaviorally proximal cardiovascular risk signal beyond overall drinks per week, while remaining more semantically stable across domains than year/state and less shortcut-prone than race. The cancer-history variables are weaker and less directly related to blood pressure.

History of non-skin cancer adds plausible, semantically stable health-status signal for hypertension risk beyond age, diabetes, smoking, activity, alcohol, and socioeconomic factors. It is less likely than survey year or state to encode domain identity, and less problematic than race as a demographic shortcut; it is also likely more relevant to blood-pressure risk than skin cancer.

Adds a modest but plausibly stable health-history signal beyond age, diabetes, smoking, and socioeconomic factors. In contrast, survey year and state are strong domain identifiers that risk shortcutting OOD splits, and race is more likely to encode demographic shortcuts and site-specific disparities than robust physiology.

Race can add some stable hypertension risk signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, smoking, activity, poverty, and employment, reflecting persistent epidemiologic differences. It is imperfect and can encode social structure, but it is still less domain-specific and less likely to cause OOD failure than survey year or state, which are strong domain identifiers and brittle shortcuts.

Survey year may capture modest secular shifts in hypertension prevalence, diagnosis, and treatment that can generalize better than geography, while STATE is primarily a domain identifier and risks encoding spurious regional patterns rather than stable physiology.

Only remaining candidate. However, state is likely to encode domain membership and regional survey artifacts more than a stable causal signal for blood pressure, so its marginal out-of-distribution value is low and potentially harmful despite capturing some real policy/environment differences.

llm_calls.content: {"selected_feature_id":11,"rationale":"Poverty adds stable socioeconomic risk information for hypertension beyond age, diabetes, activity, medical cost, and sex. It is more semantically tied to chronic stress, diet quality, and care access than year/state identifiers or race, and is less brittle than many lifestyle proxies or downstream health-status variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":6,"rationale":"Smoking history is a well-established, semantically stable cardiovascular risk factor that adds health-behavior signal beyond age, diabetes, activity, sex, poverty, and cost barriers. It is less likely than state, year, race, or employment to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and is cleaner and more robust than current-smoking detail or alcohol variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":7,"rationale":"Current smoking intensity/status adds stable cardiovascular risk information beyond ever-smoked history, improving on SMOKE100 with a more proximal exposure signal while remaining more semantically tied to blood-pressure risk than domain-heavy variables like STATE/IYEAR or shortcut-prone demographics."}

{"selected_feature_id":12,"rationale":"Employment status adds stable health and functional-status signal beyond age, poverty, sex, smoking, activity, diabetes, and cost barriers. It is plausibly linked to hypertension through stress, disability, retirement, and ability to work, while being less domain-specific and less likely to encode benchmark split identifiers than survey year or state, and less shortcut-prone than race."}

{"selected_feature_id":3,"rationale":"Alcohol consumption is a plausible, semantically stable behavioral risk factor for hypertension that adds health-related signal beyond age, diabetes, activity, smoking, sex, poverty, and employment. It is less likely than STATE or IYEAR to encode domain identity, and less likely than race or cancer-history variables to act as demographic shortcuts or weak, indirect proxies."}

{"selected_feature_id":2,"rationale":"Vegetable consumption adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle signal for blood-pressure risk that complements age, diabetes, activity, smoking, alcohol, and socioeconomic variables already selected. It is more likely to generalize across domains than survey year/state, and is less prone to demographic shortcutting than race; it also offers broader cardiovascular relevance than the cancer-history variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":1,"rationale":"Fruit intake adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle signal for blood-pressure risk that complements vegetables, activity, smoking, alcohol, diabetes, age, and poverty. It is more likely to generalize across domains than state/year and is less prone to demographic shortcutting than race; cancer history is less directly predictive, and binge drinking is partly redundant with drinks per week."}

{"selected_feature_id":4,"rationale":"Binge drinking adds a plausible, behaviorally proximal cardiovascular risk signal beyond overall drinks per week, while remaining more semantically stable across domains than year/state and less shortcut-prone than race. The cancer-history variables are weaker and less directly related to blood pressure."}

{"selected_feature_id":9,"rationale":"History of non-skin cancer adds plausible, semantically stable health-status signal for hypertension risk beyond age, diabetes, smoking, activity, alcohol, and socioeconomic factors. It is less likely than survey year or state to encode domain identity, and less problematic than race as a demographic shortcut; it is also likely more relevant to blood-pressure risk than skin cancer."}

{"selected_feature_id":8,"rationale":"Adds a modest but plausibly stable health-history signal beyond age, diabetes, smoking, and socioeconomic factors. In contrast, survey year and state are strong domain identifiers that risk shortcutting OOD splits, and race is more likely to encode demographic shortcuts and site-specific disparities than robust physiology."}

{"selected_feature_id":16,"rationale":"Race can add some stable hypertension risk signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, smoking, activity, poverty, and employment, reflecting persistent epidemiologic differences. It is imperfect and can encode social structure, but it is still less domain-specific and less likely to cause OOD failure than survey year or state, which are strong domain identifiers and brittle shortcuts."}

{"selected_feature_id":13,"rationale":"Survey year may capture modest secular shifts in hypertension prevalence, diagnosis, and treatment that can generalize better than geography, while STATE is primarily a domain identifier and risks encoding spurious regional patterns rather than stable physiology."}

{"selected_feature_id":14,"rationale":"Only remaining candidate. However, state is likely to encode domain membership and regional survey artifacts more than a stable causal signal for blood pressure, so its marginal out-of-distribution value is low and potentially harmful despite capturing some real policy/environment differences."}
